subject: Bimodal posterior when using t-distributed errors for linear regression

messages.author: 2567ef0395c70306
messages.subject: Bimodal posterior when using t-distributed errors for linear regression
parts:
As mentioned on a couple of other threads here, I'm working on using STAN for a meta-analysis of the effect of temperature on pathogen die-off. Since we are combining data from multiple studies, we try to account for uncertainty with some rigor, acknowledging both the reported errors (imputing them if they are not reported), and the number of repeated measurements taken for each experiment. To reflect these data in the model estimates, I'm using a t distribution to calculate the likelihood of the model given the data and their uncertainty, like so:

regression function: ln(Conc(t))=ln(Conc(0))-K*t

declaration in STAN with scaled data: Conc_s~student_t(df,mu_ln_Conc0-Klin_s*Time_s, sigma_C_s); 

where df is set to the number of repeated observations at each time point minus one. 

For experiments where pathogens die off in a biphasic pattern, the posterior estimates of K do not converge. Instead, the sampler seems to get stuck in a region that describes the fast rate of decay fairly well, occasionally jumping to the region that describes the line of best fit to all the data, but seeming not to explore the parameter space between these regions in a steady fashion. Is there some reason why this would be an expected behavior? I understand that using a t distribution with low degrees of freedom will make the data far less informative than using the standard normal distribution would (and indeed if I use the normal distribution instead, the model converges to the line of best fit), but I would have thought that the resulting posterior estimates would just be wider, rather than multi-modal.

The distribution of the posterior mean if you have data assumed to be t-distributed is going to be multi-modal (this shows up in some examples in Christian Robert's Bayesian choice), particularly for small numbers of degrees of freedom and a small number of samples.  If you have a larger number of samples or larger degrees of freedom this gets masked unless you have severe "outliers".  .. there are a bunch of other situations with the t distribution where you can get multi-modality.  The intuition here is that with heavy tails there are multiple alternative explanations that are (in your case) equally good.  Unfortunately multi-modality with a deep trough (as in your case, indicated by rare switching) is not something that HMC solves all that well so you have very little information about the relative mass near each mode based on the rare switching.  One solution if you can code your posterior outside of Stan is to use the HMC samples as your importance sampling distribution in importance sampling to correctly re-weight the modes.  It might be less trouble to re-parameterize but I can't come up with the right thing to do at the moment.

Krzysztof

I understand that using a t distribution with low degrees of freedom will make the data far less informative than using the standard normal distribution would (and indeed if I use the normal distribution instead, the model converges to the line of best fit), but I would have thought that the resulting posterior estimates would just be wider, rather than multi-modal.

messages.author: 2567ef0395c70306
messages.subject: Re: Bimodal posterior when using t-distributed errors for linear regression
parts:
Thanks Krzysztof,


      Interesting that the t distribution behaves this way. Subjectively, it seemed to me like the model was choosing to omit the data from the tail of the die-off some of the time, which is exactly what you've described. I'm not sure why it wouldn't also sometimes choose to omit the data from the beginning of the curve and fit only to the tail, or why there is such a deep trough between fitting only the first data or fitting all the data - I would think that, since the likelihood around each data point is heavily tailed, multiple lines that would fit on a spectrum from matching the beginning of the curve extremely to matching the end of the curve extremely well. I guess that would happen if I didn't anchor the intercept, but with an anchored intercept, the density clumps around either the line that only matches the first data but has many residuals close to 0, or the line of best fit to all the data... 

    There's a section in the STAN user manual about reparameterizing the t distribution as a normal distribution with gamma distributed standard deviation based on the degrees of freedom. I tried implementing this, but with low degrees of freedom, the scale of the gamma distribution is very large and I was getting lots of divergent transitions. 

    The key problem here for what I'm trying to do, though, is that we are really only interested in the line of best fit to the data in this model - we have another model that explicitly fits the two different regions of biphasic data. So I will have to think about an acceptable compromise that will avoid this type of bimodal posterior but can account in some way for our knowledge about the degree of uncertainty in the various data sources as we try to integrate them.

  Phil

Well, the model might have three modes HMC isn't necessarily going to find the third mode.  Another fun context where this comes up is partially observed t-distributed random walks with missing observations.  You can get 3+ modes per missing segment of observations.
or why there is such a deep trough between fitting only the first data or fitting all the data

Think of the modes as alternative explanations.  The parameter space in between the modes doesn't make sense as an explanation (according to the model).  The other thing to check in this situation is whether the model does a good job of representing the data---when you have this kind of multi-modality sometimes it's just because the model explains so little of the data.  

To simplify this have you tried fitting this model with normal distributions assumed all around? Do some model checking at that stage and make sure it says something sensible and you see the problem the t-distribution is needed for.  It's much easier to take a well-behaved model and drop something difficult like heavy tailed distributions into it rather than starting from there.

messages.author: 2567ef0395c70306
messages.subject: Re: Bimodal posterior when using t-distributed errors for linear regression
parts:
Thanks again Krzysztof,

To make things a bit clearer, this particular example is fitting a line to these data


There's an assumption built into the model that the initial concentration is fairly accurately reported, and so the intercept of the line can only vary in a relatively narrow range around the first point. For that reason, I think that the model won't fit to only the last five points, as I was speculating in the previous post. I'm still a bit surprised that the likelihood of slopes between the one that fits the first ~7 points and the one pictured above is so low, but I suppose it makes sense.


If I replace the t distributions with normal distributions in the model, the model is well behaved and returns a posterior estimate reflecting the line of best fit above. However, the next step is to use a more complex model to estimate effects of temperature on the slope of the line across many experiments, and in this setting, the relative uncertainty from all the experimental data incorporated may be important.

Yes, this is essentially an incorrect model for the data, but we're interested in fitting it because it is common practice to impose an assumption of monophasic die-off in environmental models and risk assessment frameworks because expressions for multiphasic decay are much more difficult to work with, because the proper way to relate the parameters of such expressions to external factors, such as temperature is unclear, and because the mechanisms of multiphasic decay are poorly understood, so it is unclear how to evaluate monophasic and multiphasic data in the same framework.

I don't expect the model integrating data across experiments will resolve the multimodal posteriors, because it adds to the complexity by including a relationship between K (the slope) and temperature, and also because there seems to be a lot of noise in the K~temperature relationship for this particular pathogen, maybe even to the point where there is no K~temperature relationship below 45 degrees C.

I've found an ad hoc way to approximate the uncertainty associated with small numbers of repeated observations by using an empirical function to relate mean standard deviations of the normal distributions of best fit to t distributions, given the degrees of freedom:

sigma_C_t<-(1+1060950*exp(-5.524948*df)).*sigma_C_s;

This seems to do the trick in terms of avoiding multi modality, although there are a handful of divergent transitions in each run.
